Astle CM.sub: The Jackson Laboratory · Bar Harbor, Maine, USA
story: In the Atlas, Clinton Astle is a middle author on 5 papers from the National Institute on Aging Interventions Testing Program, which tests whether drugs lengthen life in genetically mixed mice at three sites. Together they show that rapamycin extended lifespan in mice, with a bigger effect in females and at higher doses, that acarbose helped mainly males, and that resveratrol, simvastatin and several other popular compounds did not change lifespan. All of this is mouse work.
PubMed lists no affiliation for Clinton Astle in these records. A 2016 paper from the same program, sharing several co-authors, lists him at The Jackson Laboratory in Bar Harbor, Maine.

story: Two Atlas studies list Kivanç Birsoy as a middle author. One catalogued cancer-linked MTOR mutations, found 33 that switch the pathway on, and showed that cancer cells carrying them were more sensitive to rapamycin in cell culture and in mouse xenografts. The other, in mice, found that calorie restriction lowers mTORC1 activity in Paneth cells of the gut and that this boosts the intestinal stem cells next to them.

PubMed lists no affiliation for him in either record. A 2012 paper on which he is first author shares four co-authors with these studies and places him at the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

highlights.GRA2014: Middle author of the paper cataloguing hyperactivating cancer-associated MTOR mutations.
highlights.YIL2012: Middle author of the mouse study linking mTORC1 in Paneth cells to calorie restriction and stem-cell function.

Cornu M.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel · Basel, Switzerland
story: Two Atlas studies list Marion Cornu as a middle author. In mice lacking rictor (a part of mTORC2) only in the liver, the liver could not tell that the animal had eaten, so it kept making glucose and made less fat. The other study, in cells, used phosphoproteomics to show that mTORC1 switches on the building of pyrimidines, the raw material for DNA and RNA.
PubMed lists no affiliation for her in either record. A 2014 paper on which she is first author shares three co-authors with each study and places her at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel.

highlights.HAG2012: Middle author of the liver-specific rictor knockout study on mTORC2, glycolysis and fat synthesis.
highlights.ROB2013: Middle author of the phosphoproteomics study linking mTORC1 to de novo pyrimidine synthesis.

story: Two Atlas studies list Nadine Cybulski as a middle author. In one, mice lacking rictor (a part of mTORC2) only in the liver became high in blood sugar and insulin because the liver could not sense that the animal had eaten. In the other, mice lacking raptor (a part of mTORC1) in fat tissue were lean and burned more energy in their mitochondria.

PubMed lists no affiliation for her in either record. A 2009 paper on which she is first author shares several co-authors with both studies and places her at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel.

highlights.HAG2012: Middle author of the liver-specific rictor knockout study on mTORC2 and metabolism.
highlights.POL2008: Middle author of the adipose-specific raptor knockout study in lean mice.

story: Two Atlas studies list Sujuti Hidayat as a middle author. Both are cell-biology papers on raptor, the protein that sits beside mTOR. One showed that raptor is needed for mTOR to act on 4E-BP1 and S6K1, and that silencing it in worms mimics loss of TOR. The other showed that raptor grabs these two substrates through a short TOS motif.

PubMed lists no affiliation for him in these records. A 2003 paper on which he is first author shares four co-authors with both studies and places him at the Biosignal Research Center of Kobe University.

highlights.HARA2002: Middle author of the Cell paper that identified raptor as essential for mTOR action.
highlights.NOJ2003: Middle author of the paper showing raptor binds S6K1 and 4E-BP1 through their TOS motifs.
